lines.text: Incognito mode doesn't make you invisible.
lines.see: Tight on a glowing laptop browser window wearing a hat and glasses, slow push

lines.text: It only makes your own laptop forget.
lines.see: History cards stacked beside the laptop drop into a shredder and dissolve

lines.text: Here's the weird part. Everything else still sees you.
lines.see: Camera swings behind the laptop: a cable of light runs out of the room into the dark

lines.text: Every page you open leaves as a packet with your address on it.
lines.see: Amber packets fly out along the cable, each with an address tag, camera rides with them

lines.text: Your Wi-Fi, your employer, your internet provider. They all see it pass.
lines.see: Packets pass through a router, an office tower and an ISP hub, each lights up as they pass

lines.text: And the sites you visit? Google's own help page says they may too.
lines.see: Packets arrive at a wall of servers, each rack writes a glowing log line, headline quote

lines.text: In 2020, users sued Google for five billion dollars over it.
lines.see: Headline $5B counts up over the server wall

lines.text: Even inside Google, one engineer wrote: stop calling it Incognito.
lines.see: A chat bubble glows inside the server room, the hat and glasses icon flickers

lines.text: In 2024, Google agreed to delete or anonymise billions of records.
lines.see: The server log wall shreds row by row, crane up over the whole field of racks

lines.text: And the welcome screen changed. From browse privately, to browse more privately.
lines.see: Fly back along the cable to the laptop screen, the words 'more privately' swap in

lines.text: So who were you actually hiding from?
lines.see: Back to the same laptop in the hat and glasses (loop to frame 0), question headline, comment bubble

facts.claim: Google's Chrome Help page: in Incognito, Chrome doesn't retain site data or a record of the sites you visited after you close it; websites you visit, including Google sites, and organisations that manage your network, like your school, employer or Internet service provider, may be able to observe your activity
Brown v. Google (N.D. Cal., No. 20-cv-03664), filed in 2020, sought $5 billion; users alleged Google's analytics, cookies and apps tracked them in private browsing modes

Settlement terms filed 1 April 2024: Google agreed to destroy or de-identify billions of data records, update its Incognito disclosures and let Incognito users block third-party cookies for five years; no damages paid to the class (users may sue individually); covers about 136 million US users
Google changed the Incognito opening screen from 'now you can browse privately' to 'you can browse more privately'

Court documents viewed by Bloomberg: a Google engineer wrote in a 2018 chat 'We need to stop calling it Incognito and stop using a Spy Guy icon'; marketing chief Lorraine Twohill wrote to Sundar Pichai 'Make Incognito Mode truly private'
Google said it supports final approval but disputes the plaintiffs' characterisations; spokesman Jose Castaneda: 'The plaintiffs originally wanted $5 billion and are receiving zero'

publish.title: Incognito mode doesn't hide you #shorts
publish.caption:
Incognito only makes your own device forget. Your network, your employer, your internet provider and the sites you visit can still see you. In 2024 Google agreed to delete or anonymise billions of records to settle a $5 billion lawsuit.

So who were you hiding from? 👇
